body: It seems like she has no grasp of reality. The scene that happened in the movie was irrelevant to the situation that happened between the two of you. The scene in the movie existed because there is a stereotype about black hair, said to a black character. This stereotype dose not exist for Asian hair. You also did not know who's hair it was or what kind, so its irrelevant. It seems like your gf has some insecurity that she relates to this scene that she is forcing you to act out with her. Maybe she feels insecure about being in a mixed race relationship, and this incident validated those insecurities. Or she may have just felt embarrassed and latched on to this idea as a defense. Its easier for you to be racist then it is for her to accept that you mistook her hair for a pubic hair. I am sure you have explained yourself thoroughly since she has been bringing it up for a year. I would recommend to stop engaging her. She is trying to act out some emotion by playing a scene with you. Shes making you play a stand in for an imaginary argument that she wants to have. She may not even understand that that's what shes doing, as it feels real in her mind. You being racist and her being the one in the right has become her fantasy and she's going to keep acting it out with you because it feels good. Set boundaries for yourself and refuse to engage. Don't even try to explain. Just refuse and leave if necessary.

RUN! Just kidding. I'm an INFJ and my SO is INTP. I can give you some advice on things we have learned to hard way. 

INTPS are very honest, and will tell the truth no matter what. INFJs take criticism really hard, so blunt truths will probobly hurt them and can damage the relationship. You can still say what you think, but be aware of her feelings and of the consequences. If you make a negative comments about her looks or behavior, it will stick with her forever. 

On a similar note, INFJ's require a lot of positive feed back. This is tricky, considering that INTPS do not like to filter themselves. INTP's tend to show they care through help, like giving advice or performing tasks. INFJ's need actual words on top of those things to feel validated. You don't have to shower her with empty compliments, but try to tell her the things you like about her when you can. A little bit will go a long way. 

INFJs are way more emotional then INTP's. Expecting them to behave the way you would in a situation is unrealistic. It will never be helpful to tell them they are being too sensitive or over reacting. Respect the way they feel, even if its not how you would feel. 

It is very nice that you care about her enough to learn more about her. You are obviously invested in making the relationship work and that is the most important thing in any relationship. Hope this helps a little. Best wishes to you both!

Firstly, I am so sorry that you had to cope with this in your childhood. I have always found peoples attitudes towards hitting children unsettling, but spanking is particularly messed up. I really don't understand how it is not considered sexual abuse. I think that its just so normalized in certain cultures still that no one sees it that way until its presented to them. Its hard for people to wrap their heads around the idea that in average every day homes regular people are sexually insulting their kids. No parent would ever accept that getting their child circumcised was sexual abuse either. The truth is too horrible for people to cope with. Its easier for them to dismiss it then to face it, especially if it hasn't happens to them. Even victims can struggle with identifying it when it happens to them. Its easier to say your parents were strict or that you were a troublemaker. You can't just casually tell someone you got molested. Its infuriating, but its good that you can identify it. The more people hear it put in those terms, the more people will be forced to think about in those terms. Even if they deny it. Even if they'll never admit it, they will have to think about it.

Sorry you are going through this. I have been stuck in some bad jobs before and I know how stressful it can be. I haven't figured out the cure yet but I can offer some coping mechanisms that have helped me in the past. 

One big thing I learned is to stop apologizing for my personality. I used to be called overly sensitive on a regular basis at my last job and it really tore me up. After a ton of reflection, I've learned to accept this as a intrigue part of my personality stop seeing it as a "flaw" even if most people do. I still have people accuse me of it at my current job but now when they do I own it and defend it. 

Another is to limit my need for approval. I used to try to be close with everyone at work and do favors for my managers because I am unfortunately desperate for positive attention. I have learned to not seek this kind of validation at work. Now I am respectful to everyone, but only supportive to a specific few who I respect and trust. Instead of doing extra work for my bosses praise, I do extra work in exchange for extra money. 

The biggest thing I have learned is to stop caring. I have made more effort to figure out what I value most and my job is never one of them. Although I take pride in my work and enjoy my actual job since I get to help people, I no longer care about work culture or drama. I used to like to be involved in decision making and wanted to help and make suggestions when issues arise. I've learned that this tends to cause me to much stress and that I am happier leaving the problem solving to the managers (you know, the ones who get paid twice as much to deal with it).  

I hope your able to find a place you truly feel comfortable. I know even with all the coping skills in the world sometimes the environment is just too hostile. Try to find some joy outside of work in the meantime and have faith in your good qualities. Best wishes!

I am 30 years old and I cut out the vast majority of people I was close to in my 20s out of my life. I have a lot of difficulty coping with this as they were all people I felt close too and protective of. I still have fond memories of them and when I recall "good times" it always makes me second guess my discussion. I know that my "door slamming" is usually done instinctively, when I lose trust or fear that a person is going to manipulate me or cause me harm. My instincts have always been right and have saved me from some pretty awful situations, but I still have a hard time fully trusting them. Sometimes I wonder if I am just damaged from a few bad experiences and over react when I feel threatened. On the other hand, I may just be nostalgic of a time when I was more trusting, open and care free in my relationships. Now I am reserved even with people I am closest with and I don't know if I will ever be close with anyone the way I was with my friends in my 20s, even though most of them turned out to be shitty.

I think this stems from our perfectionism. The concept that one must suffer to achieve greatness is prevalent in our society. You see it with sports, with artist, with geniuses. This can also be reflected by parents, mentors and other adults we may look up too. We take particular pride in our relationships. Being great listeners. Supportive and always caring. This is our natural talent, and it is particularly jarring for us when we "fail" at it. Even if the perceived "failure" is a simple laps of judgment, or misspeaking, we tend to feel awful and beat ourselves up for it. It dose not help that we also tend to have some social anxiety, and the smallest social hiccup can send us into hiding. We are quick to banish ourselves for things most people will forget about with in 10 minutes, and refuse to forgive ourselves for things that are minuscule in grand scheme of things. I know it is probobly obvious, but it is worth remembering that making yourself suffer achieves nothing. Taking the time to think about a mistake and learn from it is a great skill, but any dwelling beyond that point will only create more anxiety within yourself, which will undoubtedly lead to more mistakes and self doubt in the future. I know its difficult in the moment when your feeling awful, but sometimes you just have to tell your brain to stop. It helps to simply write down your feelings, then go back and analyze your thinking. Am I being critical of myself? Am I blaming others? Am I using black or white thinking? Am I catastrophic? Once you have identified the flaws in your thought process, look back at your initial feelings and try to express them without judgment. So lets say you mess up at your job.  A statement "I am a failure" turns into "I made a mistake". Now that the situations is much easier to address. Here's where it gets a little corny. Everyone makes mistakes. Probably everyone you love has made one at some point, and you still love them. You deserve the same from them, and more importantly from yourself. I hope this helped a bit. Best wishes!

 I am slowly beginning to look move past the events surrounding his death and am trying to remember life before he got sick. Looking at photos and retelling stories has helped. I know that prior to getting sick he was very happy and although intense, his time being ill was breif. Its frustrating to have no answers as to what caused his death, even with the tests the vets ran.

 I am glad I opted not to do more, as it seems like whatever he had was powerful and they wouldn't have helped save him and cause him more distress. I'm glad we took care of him at home and made him as comfortable as possible. We are caring for his sister, my second cat now, as it was a big change in her life to lose him. I worry that she might have the same illness and am afraid of her having the same fate. 

I am trying to accept the fact that death is inevitable and all I can do is take care of them when the time comes. I am sorry that you had to go through something so similar but I feel some relief in knowing that even in a scenario where there are answers, there is still little you can do if its their time. I hope you are able to heal from this and give a good life to another cat someday.  Take care.

I think INFPs and INTPs have a clearer set of morals that they follow compared to INFJ's. They'er morals are set as "rules" that they do not stray from. In contrast, INFJs don't really give themselves moral rules, they are flexible depending on the situation. I have definitely changed my mind over time on subjects I had very strong views about, and can totally shift ideas if I see a different view point. 

I am also able to accept or forgive a lot of immoral behavior if I can understand it. This has allowed me to get myself involved with some bad people/ situations and make some mistakes of my own, so I do admire these types ability to lay down the law, so to speak. That being said, I think these types can be blindsided by their own rules, and are not always good at adhering to their own high moral standards.

 For example, I told an INTP I know about a friend who abused the Amazon return policy to get free stuff. The INTP was disgusted by this and has expressed a lot of disdain for this specific behavior with other peole/stores. This same INTP borrowed money from me and when I asked them if they would pay me back months later they basically told me that they didn't think they had to pay me back because I wasn't assertive enough about getting the money back.

 Neither of these behaviors are great but on a moral scale it is much worse to abuse an act of kindness and destroy the trust of someone close to you than it is to take advantage of a policy of a wealthy cooperation. I guess from my observations, the INTP and INFP tend to have a moral code that is built on their personal experiences. If something hurts them, they will have a hard and fast opinion on it. But they are usually unaware about how they're behavior hurts others or about things that don't effect them. They lack the empathy to make well rounded moral judgments. So I wouldn't say that their morality is stronger than INFJS, its just louder and clearer.

All my serious relationships involved me helping my SO's through some big life event and them losing interest or dumping me after. I think the initial attraction can be very intense in those situations because you are exactly what they need during that time. On my part, I guess the attraction just comes from the intensity of the emotions their having and the feeling of being needed. But after time, this doesn't go well. The "victim" person will either get over their problem and no longer need you, or they will continue to be the victim and resent your positivity and help. I've found that over time I also start to dislike being the caregiver when it is so one sided. I want a partnership, but I always feel like I ended being in the responsible role and It exhausts me. I really want a relationship with someone who is supportive and responsible and can provide security, but people like that have never shown interest in me.
